result.audience_type: STEM undergraduates, mathematically curious professionals (engineers, designers, educators), and serious self-taught learners with solid quantitative foundations. The common thread is comfort with mathematical reasoning and genuine curiosity about the geometry of folding -- not exam pressure or research deadlines. This includes math or CS undergrads looking for enrichment, working engineers interested in deployable structures or metamaterials, educators who want to teach math through origami, and hobbyist folders who want to understand the theory behind what their hands already do.
result.goal: Build working fluency in origami mathematics: understand, state, and apply the core theorems (Kawasaki-Justin, Maekawa) and axioms (Huzita-Justin), reason about flat-foldability and geometric constructibility, and connect paper-folding to broader mathematical structures. The student should finish able to read primary literature (Hull's Origametry, key papers), use computational tools (Origami Simulator, TreeMaker), and recognize origami-mathematical structure in engineering applications. This is intellectual enrichment with enough rigor to serve as a launchpad into deeper study, not a terminal survey.
result.background: Comfortable with algebra, coordinate geometry, and trigonometry. Some exposure to proof-based mathematics -- at minimum one college-level course in discrete math, linear algebra, or an introduction-to-proofs course (or equivalent self-study). Familiarity with basic calculus (derivatives, integrals) is helpful for selected topics (curved folds, optimization in circle packing) but not a hard prerequisite for most of the curriculum. No prior knowledge of origami technique is required, though some hands-on folding experience helps ground the abstractions. No programming background assumed, though computationally inclined students will get more from the algorithmic modules.
result.tone: Hands-on and example-driven, with formal foundations introduced through physical intuition. Every theorem should first be discovered through folding before being stated precisely. Rigorous where it matters -- theorems stated with full conditions, key proofs worked through step by step -- but never formalism for its own sake. Conversational enough to sustain daily self-study, precise enough that the student builds real mathematical vocabulary. Rabbit holes encouraged: connections to Galois theory, NP-hardness, space engineering, and metamaterials should appear as fascinating asides that reward curiosity without derailing the main thread.
result.depth: Intuition plus key proofs, with applied grounding. Build geometric intuition through physical folding, then formalize with precise theorem statements and selected complete proofs (e.g., Kawasaki's theorem, the constructibility of angle trisection via Axiom 6). Provide proof sketches or guided outlines for harder results (NP-hardness of flat-foldability, origami number hierarchy) rather than full formal treatments. Include computational exercises using Origami Simulator and hands-on folding tasks alongside written problems. The student should understand why results are true, not just what they say, but the course stops short of the full graduate treatment found in Demaine-O'Rourke or Hull's Origametry.
result.time_commitment: 10-15 minutes of study (reading, worked examples, watching short demonstrations) plus 10-15 minutes of exercises (a mix of written mathematical problems and physical folding tasks). Some lessons will designate a hands-on folding component requiring a sheet of paper, adding 5-10 minutes. Total per lesson: 25-40 minutes, consistent with the 1% daily growth rule. Heavier sessions (e.g., a full proof walkthrough or a simulator exploration) should be flagged in advance so the student can plan accordingly.
